claims.text: Previous HVAF-M3 depositions used FeCoNiCrAl powder with a 15–45 μm particle-size range.
Standard HVAF-i7 processing of 15–45 μm FeCoNiCrAl produces acceptable coating quality but inadequate thickness.
Adjusting HVAF-i7 gas flow and stand-off distance can increase in-flight particle velocity.
A nozzle-specific spray distance of approximately 300–350 mm is suitable for obtaining enhanced particle velocity.
Conventional MCrAlY studies show that increased particle velocity enhances deposition efficiency.
Greater particle kinetic energy improves impact and splat formation.
Improved impact and splat formation increase bonding and packing efficiency at the substrate.
Higher particle velocity reduces the particles' high-temperature in-flight residence time.
Reducing high-temperature in-flight residence time limits oxidative exposure.
Higher particle momentum enhances splat flattening and coalescence.
Enhanced splat flattening and coalescence produce a thicker, denser FeCoNiCrAl coating.
Increasing particle velocity during HVAF-i7 processing will increase FeCoNiCrAl deposition efficiency.
The adjusted process will produce a noticeably thicker FeCoNiCrAl bond coat than standard HVAF-i7 processing of the same 15–45 μm feedstock.
The thicker coating will remain well adhered.
The adjusted process will retain low as-sprayed oxidation despite the increased particle velocity.
The resulting coating will meet high-temperature thermal-barrier durability requirements.
The intervention should remain effective for deposition within internal diameters as small as approximately 120 mm.
The intervention remains viable only if increased velocity does not increase oxidation or cause deleterious thermal effects.

The proposed experiment compares standard and velocity-enhanced HVAF-i7 depositions using the same FeCoNiCrAl powder size range and evaluates thickness, adhesion, oxidation, phases, porosity, and microstructural integrity.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant thickness increase while maintaining adhesion and similar oxidation levels would falsify the hypothesis.
